analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to knowingly sell a dangerous defective product and opens secret court settlements about safety hazards.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced weeks after the Firestone tire recall, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a vote, and died when Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have done three things. First, it would have made it a federal crime, punishable by up to 15 years in prison, for a company to knowingly put a defective product into commerce or to hide a known defect from regulators after someone is hurt. Second, it would have stopped federal courts from routinely sealing evidence and settlements that hide health and safety hazards from the public. Third, it would have tightened auto safety law: makers would have to investigate crashes for possible defects, notify regulators of suspected problems, cover defect repairs for longer, and pay up to $10,000 per safety violation instead of $1,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and vehicle owners, who would be warned earlier about dangerous defects, get free repairs for longer, and see safety evidence that companies currently keep sealed in lawsuit settlements. People injured by hidden hazards, and regulators who would learn of defects sooner, also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, up to 15 years in prison when a known defect kills someone and up to 5 years for serious injury, for a company to knowingly distribute a defective product or to intentionally fail to disclose a known defect to regulators [S3].

Bars federal courts from approving secrecy orders or settlements that hide information relevant to public health or safety unless the confidentiality interest clearly outweighs the public interest in disclosure, and forbids courts from enforcing agreements that block parties from reporting hazards to federal or state agencies [S3].

Requires motor vehicle and equipment manufacturers to review accident and incident information, including foreign sources, and notify the Transportation Secretary when they have reason to believe a defect may exist [S3].

Extends the period during which manufacturers must fix defects at no charge from 8 to 10 calendar years (or 3 to 5 years for equipment), raises the per-violation civil penalty from $1,000 to $10,000, and requires manufacturers to certify compliance only after conducting appropriate testing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, tire and auto-parts makers, and other consumer product manufacturers, which would face criminal exposure for knowingly dangerous products, tenfold higher civil penalties, longer free-repair obligations, and less ability to seal settlement evidence. Some of these costs would be passed to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The criminal provision uses a broad definition of 'defective product' — any flaw that makes a product dangerous beyond the reasonable and accepted risk — and applying criminal penalties to ordinary manufacturing decisions could chill product development or expose executives to prison over debatable engineering judgments [S3].

Critics of such measures argue that defective products already face civil lawsuits, recalls, and regulatory penalties, so adding criminal liability duplicates existing remedies and raises costs that flow into consumer prices; the bill itself acknowledges cost by extending mandatory free repairs to 10 years for vehicles [S3].

Restricting protective orders and sealed settlements can also expose legitimate trade secrets, which is why the bill requires courts to weigh the confidentiality interest against the public interest rather than banning secrecy outright [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety upside is substantial: earlier disclosure of defects, longer free repairs, real criminal consequences for knowingly hiding dangers, and an end to court orders that bury hazard evidence. The main cost falls on manufacturers, some of it passed to consumers as prices. The criminal provision is drafted broadly enough that it could reach judgment calls rather than only deliberate concealment, which is the strongest honest objection; the secrecy provisions are narrower and already required courts to weigh confidentiality.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein, joined by Sen. Herb Kohl, introduced the bill on September 19, 2000 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill got one cosponsor and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or House action before the Congress expired [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto and consumer product manufacturers, which avoided new criminal penalties, tenfold higher civil fines, longer free-repair duties, and court rules that would have unsealed hazard evidence in settlements.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2000 and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-run committee that could have acted never did.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle and auto equipment manufacturers (cars, tires, parts)
industries.note: The bill would have created criminal exposure for knowingly shipping defective vehicles and parts, required makers to investigate crashes and report suspected defects, doubled-to-quinbled... raised civil penalties tenfold to $10,000 per violation, and extended mandatory free defect repairs from 8 to 10 years. Its interest in avoiding those duties ran against the public's interest in safer vehicles.

industries.industry: Broader consumer product manufacturers and litigation defendants
industries.note: The Sunshine in Litigation provisions would have sharply limited courts' willingness to seal discovery and settlements, and barred enforcing agreements that stop parties from reporting hazards to regulators. Companies that used confidentiality agreements to keep hazard evidence out of public view would lose that shield.
